Centering theory, which focuses on identifying a central entity or situation in discourse, has been examined through various methods including corpus analysis and computational frameworks. We investigate the connection between centering theory and a modern neural reference resolution system by analyzing the predictive capabilities of features derived from this theory. Our study takes the BART S2 T5 reference resolution model and examines the importance of conditionals, inferences, and entity features in predicting reference annotations. We find that the predictive power of conditionals and inferences associated with the center easily expires (R-expiration), the marginal entity feature, and the post-center conditionals is zero. We also observe that R-expiration is a persistent phenomenon across discourse lengths and can be a crucial aspect of the theory, providing a nuanced understanding of the concept of centrality.

Recently, outdoor range assessment has been a subject of interest for the artificial intelligence community, particularly in relation to self-driving applications. Researchers have explored the use of machine learning models to predict distances from Wi-Fi access points, considering various factors such as signal strength and map data. However, these models have not been shown to account for the effects of obstacles and terrain on range assessment, which are critical variables in outdoor navigation. To address this limitation, a novel approach has been presented that utilizes a combination of machine learning and physics-based modeling to accurately estimate outdoor ranges. The proposed method employs a two-tier approach, beginning with the use of a support vector machine to identify categories of access points based on their characteristics, followed by an assessment of the range using a physics-based model that takes into account the effects of obstacles and terrain. The results have demonstrated that the proposed method can estimate ranges with a mean absolute error of 1.43 meters, outperforming existing models and providing a foundation for further integration with navigation systems.

The Beam Fragmentation Instability (BFI) problem in Energy Recovery Linacs (ERLs) remains an obstacle due to the recirculation of electrons interacting with small numbers of circulating bunches. As ERL designs often feature multiple recirculations and non-overlapping bunch trains, research has focused on the effects of filling configurations on BFI. A previous study demonstrated the importance of taking into account the effects of beam-beam interactions in multiple passes to assess BFI accurately. It showed that in an eight-pass case, the average tune shift of about 1.3 could become as high as 4.5, varying greatly with filling configurations. To enhance stability, it's proposed to employ a recirculation scheme with overlapping bunch trains, which can also be beneficial for improving beam utilization. A more complex eight-pass case with filling configurations featuring up to nine bunch trains was analyzed, and it was discovered that this scheme can reduce the average number of beam-beam interactions in multiple passes by two to three times, resulting in an increase in the stability limit from about 10 MV to 30 MV. To achieve greater levels of stability with current technology, it's recommended to design recirculation schemes with filling configurations that minimize beam-beam interactions in multiple passes, and to explore options for mitigating BFI through methods such as emittance enhancement and non-overlapping bunch train designs.

Using the BFKT formalism, we expanded the one-loop amplitude for two gluons in N=4 SYM theory, expressing it through a set of elementary building blocks - two gluon central-emission vertices and a pair of gluon "mermaid" diagrams with two collinear gluons. We calculated the one-loop amplitude in two different approaches: directly from the one-loop amplitude and by reconstructing it from the pre-defined building blocks. We found that the one-loop amplitude for two gluons in N=4 SYM theory equals one half the sum of the square of the color-ordered two-gluon amplitude and the reconstructed amplitude from the pair of "mermaid" diagrams. We also validated our results by analyzing the one-loop amplitude for two gluons in N=4 SYM theory in the limit of large rapidity separation, where it equals one half the sum of the square of the BES one-loop amplitude.

Research has shown that the end regions of polymer chains experience abnormally high resistance to flow, a phenomenon known as the "free end effect." Studies have primarily focused on linear polymer bristles, but the project described here involves using computational methods to study non-linear polymer bristles under stress by simulating the flow of a polymer melt in a shear flow experiment. By analyzing the local velocity profiles near the ends of the bristles, we identified areas with slowed velocity, which were more extensive at the points where the bristles met an obstacle than at free ends. This research provides equations that describe these end regions for any shaped bristles, both curved and complex, and it shows that the free end effect can be eliminated if the bristles are curved in a way that creates recirculation zones, even at low shear rates.

A graph G is considered visible from a location w if there's a path connecting w to every vertex in G. The visible diameter of G at a site v is the maximum distance from v to any other vertex in G. The shortened metric dimension of a graph G, denoted by sdim(G), is the minimum number required to determine the distinct distances to all other vertices in G, considering the visible diameter. Our study delves into the exploration of shortened diamond dimensions for various types of graphs, including those with a specific parameter distance, as well as pseudo-regular graphs where every vertex has the same neighbourhood size, and the resulting dimension after removing a minimum number of vertices while keeping the desired property.

Researchers employed a machine learning technique to analyze all-sky maps of gamma radiation using the Fermi-LAT telescope. By leveraging random forests, they reprocessed the map while identifying variable sources and accounting for instrumental backgrounds. This led to a 2.5 times improvement in detecting weak sources and enabled the discovery of over 100 new variable sources, primarily with a periodic pattern likely linked to binary systems. This approach's effectiveness in the center of the galaxy was particularly notable, where it significantly reduced the source count by removingscattered photons from the galaxy while preserving local sources.

In a serial dictatorship where one person makes decisions for an interval representing a group of people, adding a mechanism for individual preferences to influence decisions within that interval can be counterproductive, potentially leading to outcomes worse than the status quo. However, under specific conditions such as when the interval represents a society with varying levels of risk tolerance or certain production scenarios, over time (in a sense that includes serially) relative to dictatorial decision-making can lead to socially better results.

We conducted a survey of binary asteroids using images from the Pan-STARRS1 wide-field telescope, which captured high-resolution photographs of 46 distinct asteroids, including 601, 162943, 2001 VX6, 216 KElmira, 390 Althea, 45 Eugenia, 67 Assyria, 15 Eulimene, 3 Juno, 4 Vesta, 6 Hebe, 15 Eulimene B, 16 Psyche, 18 Melpomene, 45 Eugenia, 52 Europa, 67 Assyria, 70 Antiope, 76 Geometria, 87 Sylvia, 121 Hermione, 162943, 2001 VX7, 216 KElmira, 390 Althea, 45 Eugenia, 67 Assyria, 15 Eulimene, 3 Juno, 4 Vesta, 6 Hebe, 15 Eulimene B, 16 Psyche, 18 Melpomene, 45 Eugenia, 52 Europa, 67 Assyria, 70 Antiope, 76 Geometria, 87 Sylvia, 121 Hermione, 162943, 2001 VX7, 216 KElmara, 390 Althea, 45 Eugenia, 67 Assyria, 15 Eulimene, 3

In recent years, there has been growing interest in modeling peer influences within social networks, using linear regression as a fundamental tool for this purpose. Research has already established methods for estimating the parameters of a full linear regression model, but there's a gap in the literature for handling partially linear regression models, especially in terms of evaluating the model's validity and estimating peer effects. This study addresses these shortcomings by developing a theoretical framework for partially linear regression models, with subsequent application to estimating peer influences in networks. With simulations conducted to evaluate the proposed methods, it was found that the theoretical guarantees also hold in practice, with network peer influences then estimated using the partially linear regression framework with results showing that this approach outperforms the standard linear regression method.

This research paper aims to introduce novel variants of the Leibniz rule for the Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative operators. We have successfully established these variants and applied them to derive the variations of the Leibniz rule for the Mittag-Leffler function and related identities. Additionally, we have been able to utilize these variants to generalize the Leibniz rule for the variable-order fractional integral and derivative operators, making them specific cases of our generalised formula.

The rising popularity of interactive storytelling in fantasy settings like Dungeons and Dragons has been met with significant interest, particularly in the field of AI-generated narratives. To further explore this trend, we've developed a framework for guiding the adventure, centered around a central figure known as the Dungeon Master. In this framework, the Dungeon Master's decisions are influenced by a desire to either challenge or engage the players, which we've termed their "mindset." Our goal in creating this framework was to see if it could be used to teach a machine learning model to effectively manage the adventure's progression and the players' experiences. To accomplish this, we trained the model using a combination of reinforcement learning and intention-based dialogue, where the intention was represented by the desired outcome of the action and the mindset was a secondary factor that could be changed during the game. In testing the model, we found it to be capable of successfully guiding the adventure through multiple rounds, even when the players deviated from the planned course of action. Systematically varying the model's parameters and the game's conditions, we observed that the model's performance was significantly impacted by the complexity of the game world and the frequency with which it changed, but not by the depth of its knowledge or the extent of the players' cheating. To make the model more suitable for real-world applications, we identified several areas in need of improvement, including the need for a more sophisticated method of determining the model's knowledge base and a more reliable way to identify the players' actions

Recently developed topological methods for analyzing knotted protein structures have uncovered a variety of complex knot patterns, yet the lack of knowledge regarding the environmental contexts of protein knots limits their biological significance. In this study, we used a novel approach to examine the spatial relationships between protein structures and applied topological analysis to identify specific knots, ultimately classifying and quantifying protein knots based on their spatial arrangements. A significant finding revealed that certain protein knots exhibit distinct preferences for specific folding patterns, and a statistical approach revealed that certain knots are associated with specific bending pathways. Notably, our research demonstrated that certain bending pathways can accommodate various knot patterns, and our discovery of specific knots associated with planar folding patterns was particularly intriguing. Using planar proteins as a proxy for folded proteins, we developed a method to model their three-dimensional structures and applied it to a subset of proteins with a specific knot pattern known as twist knots, ultimately revealing the detailed three-dimensional arrangements of these proteins. Our research provides a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between the structure, folding, and three-dimensional arrangement of proteins and offers a novel way to examine the relationship between knot patterns and bending pathways using topological analysis.

The symplectic mapping category group associated with $\omega$, denoted as $\Gamma_{\omega}(V)$, is well-defined and consists of the set of all maps $f: V \to V$ that preserve the symplectic structure of $\omega$, together with a non-negative number $\omega_f$ as a coefficient, satisfying the properties of a category group.  In the case where the center of the group $\Gamma_{\omega}(V)$ does not contain any non-trivial subgroups of a finite order, it has been proven that $\Gamma_{\omega}(V)$ can be parameterized by a set of distinct parameters, specifically the coefficients in a certain power series defined by a generating function related to the Gelfand-Lidstone series, which completely determines the structure of $\Gamma_{\omega}(V)$ up to an isomorphism.  Some examples of parameterizing the groups $\Gamma_{\omega}(V)$ for various types of symplectic forms on the vector space $V$ have been given. The Irregular Nambu-Goldstone Theorem stands as a significant extension to the fundamental Nambu-Goldstone Theorem, allowing for a broader understanding of its underlying mechanisms. We have achieved a deeper comprehension of the INGT through an in-depth analysis of a variety of quantum field theories, both relativistic and non-relativistic in nature, by applying the concept of symmetry breaking and the resulting Higgs mechanism. We have the Einstein theory of gravity as a notable example in our study of the INGT applied to the framework of general relativity. We have also explored the effects of an invariant spacetime metric on the INGT within the context of both the standard model and its unified extensions. Furthermore, we have the Faddeev-Nemiashilai model and the Chiral Nambu-Dinertin model as non-relativistic examples of the INGT at work. We have also derived a more general form of the INGT in both its relativistic and non-relativistic forms, with an emphasis on the role of Riemannian metric symmetry. We have the Heisenberg's non-relativistic theory of hadron interactions as an example of the INGT in a non-relativistic setting. We have also explored the effects of an invariant spacetime matrix algebra on the INGT within the context of both the standard model and its unified extensions, with an emphasis on the role of finite field theory. Recent advancements in modifying language models have led to the development of counterfactual generation tasks that produce tailored training data, raising the question of what kind of data is most beneficial for machine learning models. To address this, we propose a novel method for creating phrasal counterfactuals by applying local transformations to specific words within a sentence, which we call the Discrete Decoupling Counterfactual Strategy. By modifying words in a particular syntactic context, we can condition counterfactuals on various linguistic features such as semantic roles, part-of-speech tags, and syntactic structures. To support this approach, we created the DISCO corpus, which includes over 13,000 counterfactual sentences generated for both sentence and dependency structures. In tests conducted on extensive language models, it was observed that counterfactuals conditioned on both syntactic structures and semantic roles led to improved performance compared to standard training methods.

In this research, the epitaxial growth of a quaternary Heusler compound, (Co,Ni)2AlHeusler, was examined on a graphene/sapphire substrate using a MBE system. Initially, we investigated the effects of varying the epitaxial growth method, including van der Waals epitaxy, long-range periodic epitaxy, and short-range periodic epitaxy facilitated by Au or Ni/NiO nucleation sites, on a single layer of (Co,Ni)2AlHeusler. Long-range periodic epitaxy was achieved by controlling the pinhole density in the graphene substrate. We found that the (Co,Ni)2AlHeusler layers exhibit a cubic rock-salt structure, with lattice parameters that depend on the epitaxial growth method. We also determined the magnetic properties and investigated the effects of annealing and Co/Ni doping. Notably, long-range periodic epitaxy resulted in a unique magnetic pattern on the surface, whereas short-range periodic epitaxy facilitated by Ni/NiO nucleation sites led to an irregular magnetic pattern. We examined the energy dispersive spectroscopy and Raman spectroscopy of the samples to understand the interaction between the (Co,Ni)2AlHeusler layers and the graphene/sapphire substrate. We found that long-range periodic epitaxy can be controlled by varying the vacuum pressure during transfer and the number of graphene layers, which allows for the fabrication of magnetic Heusler compounds with precise control over

Every error-correcting code can be viewed as a subspace of a specific vector space, and when considering the Hamming metric, codes that correct up to $t$ errors can be linked to the properties of a specific matrix, specifically, those related to its rank and the dimension of its null space. More specifically, the ability to correct up to $t$ errors is equivalent to the ability to detect up to $t$ column changes in a generator matrix, which in turn is equivalent to the ability to correct up to $t$ row changes in a parity-check matrix. The relationship between the Hamming distance and the row or column changes in a matrix is what motivates an examination of codes whose decoding ability is linked to the dimension of their null space, specifically those defined by the intersection of the duals of their duals being isomorphic to the additive group of integers modulo $p^2$, specifically $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$. These codes can correct up to $t$ column changes in a generator matrix, which is equivalent to correcting up to $t$ row changes in a parity-check matrix, and are therefore equivalent to having a null space of dimension $t$.

In this research, we analyze how instances are categorized based on multiple labels by using a single positive label. We rephrase this concept as "instance expansion" into multiple labels. We use a metaphorical "fingerprint" to represent instances, and "label footprint" to represent labels. We examine how instances are associated with labels, starting with a simple co-occurrence model and gradually enhance it to a more complex model that considers relationships between labels and instances. We validate our approach on multiple datasets, and it outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and F1-score.

Quantum field theory in a unified framework, as proposed by Dunne, is the basis for the presentation of a novel feature of Euclidean algebraic QFT. The feature in question is the discovery of a connection between the geometric representation of symplectic vector spaces and the Hermitian Hilbert space of the theory, defined through a specific algebraic structure. The foundation for this feature was established by Haag, Weizel, and Hepp in the context of Wightman functions, and it was further developed by Epstein, Glaser, and Osterwalder by utilizing the Feynman-Kac formula and stochastic processes. A key aspect of this feature is the relationship it shares with the concept of "physical space," which was a central element of Haag's approach to quantum field theory. The discussion of this feature also includes an examination of its implications for the vacuum state and a connection to the GNS construction from mathematical physics. The connection to the algebra of local observables, as well as the CCR algebra, is discussed in the context of Weyl-Wigner transform. The feature in question can be applied to both perturbative and non-perturbative approaches to Euclidean algebraic QFT. The paper concludes by presenting the novel feature as a key element of the Dunne framework and highlighting its potential applications to both the perturbative and non-perturbative aspects of the theory.

The nature of gamma-rays in the high-energy band remains poorly understood, particularly in the context of nearby radio galaxies.  Two types of accretion processes are thought to occur in these objects - accretion onto a black hole and onto a magnetized neutron star.  If a neutron star is present, it can be surrounded by a disk of captured magnetic field energy, which can fuel gamma-ray emission.  A study of 12 nearby radio galaxies with protons of 50 GeV or more found that the gamma-ray emission in the highest energy band can be explained by the captured magnetic field energy in the disk.  This is particularly evident in the entropy ratio of the electron population, which is abnormal for hadronic emission from a black hole.  A model is proposed in which the gamma-ray emission in the highest energy band results from the interaction of high-energy protons with a low-energy component of radiating particles, likely the captured magnetic field electrons.  This model is supported by data from two blazars, 3C 61A and NGC 6251, which also exhibit a separate component of hadronic emission from a black hole.  The proposed model is consistent with the observed emission patterns of these two blazars.

Early detection of heart conditions such as cardiac arrhythmias and valve disorders can be critical for preventing sudden death, making automated analysis of stethoscope recordings vital for emergency settings. However, on-site automated systems require the ability to accurately analyze recordings in noisy environments, which poses a significant challenge for the existing methods of analysis. This paper presents a novel approach to analyzing stethoscope recordings with the presence of background noise and an obstructive path between the sound source and the recording device. By applying a novel signal processing technique called Convolutional Conditional Deep Independent Component Analysis, this research achieves an accuracy of 93.1% in classifying heart sounds in a noisy environment, which is a 14.4% improvement over the current state of the art. By comparing the reconstructed recordings from the proposed method with the original recordings, this study also provides a visual representation of the recorded heart sounds in a way that highlights the areas of the chest associated with each valve, which can be valuable for medical professionals in localizing the source of heart sounds.

The proliferation of wearable devices and mobile internet has led to an explosion in health data collection, but the data itself is scattered, lacking utility due to privacy and security concerns. As a leading cause of death worldwide, cardiovascular disease poses a significant threat, necessitating the development of accurate, private, and efficient methods to predict high-risk cardiovascular events. Current machine learning models, despite being accurate, cannot be developed on wearable data due to its fragmented nature and cannot be developed privately without violating data privacy protocols. Our proposed FedHealth system addresses these limitations by constructing a federated transfer knowledge framework that combines local models on a federated manner, safely and efficiently, while prioritizing data privacy. FedHealth succeeds in predicting cardiovascular disease risk on a new and scattered data set, without accessing the original data, without a decrease in accuracy, without a decrease in efficiency, and while conforming to a high standard of data security protocols. Experimental results show that FedHealth achieves an AUC-ROC of 0.967, an AUC-PR of 0.956, an F1-score of 0.843, an AP of 0.944, an CP at 0.166, and an ESR of 0.037 on a publicly available wearable healthcare dataset, surpassing the performance of baseline models by a significant margin.

An investment portfolio's performance can be evaluated using various metrics, including standard deviation, worst loss, expected loss, semi-deviation, and tail conditional expectation. Researchers have examined the relationships among these measures and explored methods to optimize portfolio performance, particularly in times of market stress. Some studies suggest that the worst loss, expected loss, semi-deviation, and tail conditional expectation can be expressed in terms of skewness and semi-standard deviation, which are more readily calculable values. These expressions are applicable under both normal and non-normal distribution assumptions. By substituting these expressions into a normal distribution framework, researchers have derived equations for calculating portfolio performance measures such as worst loss, expected loss, semi-deviation, and tail conditional expectation in terms of value-at-risk. These equations can be used to calculate the skewness and semi-standard deviation of a portfolio, which can be further used to evaluate the performance of various portfolio optimization techniques under non-normal conditions.

In order to automate the process of configuring, managing, and maintaining software at scale, an automated system for handling software is required. This system should be capable of managing complex relationships between software components, resolving dependency conflicts and version incompatibilities, and ensuring security and compliance standards are met. An approach to automate the process of software configuration is proposed, starting from the initial analysis of available software packages and ending with the deployment of the configured software. This approach is under continuous development and has been applied to configure and manage various aspects of the Apache Airflow project. An examination of the challenges faced while working with Airflow is used to illustrate the proposed approach and highlight areas where improvements are needed.

This research paper focuses on a control problem where the cost function includes the number of sign changes in a certain type of adapted process. It aims to establish the equivalence of two problem formulations, one with constraints on the total variation of the control process and the other with the sign change cost. It also explores the asymptotic behavior of this problem as the sign change cost tends to zero. The paper further considers an associated stochastic control problem and provides an estimate on the minimum cost of this problem. It also discusses the connection to a problem of optimal investment with partial information. The results built upon previous research by Fajfowlak and Krzyszczyk, the doctoral dissertation by Hamel, and the master's thesis by Hamel and Hamel.

To explore the properties of massive vector bosons and certain types of leptoquarks that interact with electrons and muons, a new analysis is presented of existing LHC data featuring two leptoquark production scenarios. This study examines the potential for a specific type of leptoquark, known as scalar or vector "collective" (SC or VC) with a charge of 1 or 2, to be discovered through the process of electron-muon pair creation, particularly in events featuring same-sign lepton pairs. By applying various selection criteria to existing IET data, researchers were able to either set more stringent lower limits on the mass of these leptoquarks or determine masses within previously established ranges. For example, research was able to establish an upper limit on the mass of charge 1 SC leptoquarks at approximately 1090 GeV and set the lower limit for charge 2 VC leptoquarks at 983 GeV.

We analyzed a large database of galaxy spectra, specifically targeting the thermal CO tenors' effect on the strength of the subthermal C I lines, given that both lines are commonly used to measure the mass of molecular gas. Initially, we constructed an empirical formula for the C I line ratios based on a large spectral database, accounting for various factors such as optical depth, beam filling factor, and CO tenor. This was achieved by correlating the line ratios with the line luminosity, effectively removing the influence of optical depth. We discovered a direct relationship between the line luminosity and the line ratio, which can be described by a power law. Next, we investigated the relationship between CO tenor and the line ratio, discovering a boundary above which CO tenor prevails over C I line ratios. We found this boundary to be influenced by both star formation rate and total molecular gas mass. Notably, the line ratio is generally subthermal even in massive gas reservoirs. This is particularly significant for high mass reservoirs, which are often associated with star-bursting galaxies, as it indicates that these galaxies are still efficiently converting gas into stars. This finding has implications for the theories attempting to explain the formation of these galaxies. This research has practical applications for measuring the line ratio and hence the mass of molecular gas, especially in distant galaxies where high-resolution spectra may not be feasible to obtain, as it allows for estimating the line ratio from the line luminosity, thus circumventing the need for detailed

In 2019, a challenge was issued to the statistics community to explore a method called series reconstruction for permutations using the Hamming distance. Researchers gathered the results of attempts made during the challenge period, analyzing various approaches and combining them into three categories: (1) empirical studies based on random data sets, (2) simulated data with specific characteristics, and (3) real-world applications. An analysis of the challenges faced and lessons learned can be found in the appendix. Along with the existing literature, these results have been used to test and validate the proposed method, providing insights into its performance in different scenarios.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual mergers of binary black holes of moderate mass, particularly those with significant eccentricity. By utilizing an analytical approach, we generated a vast set of PTA data streams that mimic gravitational waves from merging binary black holes with varying levels of eccentricity, primarily of 2.25, and with a particular mass ratio of 7, by means of a numerical relativity simulation called O3gmap. We developed an analytical model to match the PTA data streams for binary black hole mergers with moderate to high eccentricity in their final stages of inspiral, near their point of merging. We found that even in the presence of significant eccentricity, the PTA signals from these mergers can be accurately described using an analytical model in the point of merging, with a precision of around one part in 10 to the power of 8. We also investigated the precision with which the analytical model can match the PTA data streams throughout the entire process of merging, with an outcome of around one part in 10 to the power of 7, by employing a strategy of comparing the analytical model with the numerical simulation data directly, without the involvement of the PTA response. We further developed an analytical approach to calculate the time and frequency characteristics of the PTA data streams, with an outcome of being able to generate the PTA data streams for all possible orientations of the binary black hole

A systematic velocity change procedure has been established for ASEP random particle systems in [from_REF], which was found to lead to conservation laws for the stochastic PDE system associated with the ASEP, and it was also shown that this procedure is reversible. Additionally, it has been demonstrated that the ASEP with initial condition defined by the step function can be transformed into the TASEP through a sequence of velocity changes, which results in the creation of clogs and eventually leads to the TASEP.

Mathematical models play a significant role in understanding the spread of infectious diseases by examining factors contributing to their rapid growth, eventual peak, and decline, as well as evaluating and comparing different intervention strategies to control outbreaks. Although data quality significantly impacts the accuracy and effectiveness of these models, it is essential to address methodological limitations and criticisms, as well as the potential misuse of models, to ensure their value in assisting public health policy is maintained. In this paper, we examine various models used to study the spread of the SARS-CoV-2 virus and emphasize the need for better data, including detailed contact patterns and mobility information, to accurately model and predict the course of the pandemic. We also discuss the potential risks of models being applied outside their valid parameters, as well as the limitations of statistical testing in evaluating model performance. Furthermore, we outline the essential components and challenges of modeling the current pandemic, with the goal of promoting a more nuanced understanding of the complex interplay between epidemiological, demographic, and economic factors, as well as the social measures and public health interventions being employed to combat the pandemic.

We've investigated a novel process where a spinless particle and two spinor atoms interact and transform into a spinor molecule and a spinless particle. This process can be driven by a combination of two laser beams with frequencies that match the energy difference between the particle and the molecule, or the energy difference between two of the molecule's levels. We've shown that in both cases, the particle-molecule transformation has a maximum efficiency when a third particle is present, which can provide an energy source through three-body recombination. This process requires that the two interacting spinor atoms have equal masses and the ability to move at similar speeds. It can occur even when they are far apart and only interact through a short-range force, and it allows for the creation of molecules with large internal energy, which could be used for quantum computing.

Recently, hierarchical data storage has been proposed to efficiently manage large amounts of data with varying levels of importance, utilizing both conventional and phase-change memory arrays. This technique has been shown to be particularly effective in reducing data retrieval time and increasing storage durability. However, one flaw in this design is the lack of a well-defined protocol for updating the memory hierarchy, specifically the DNA information layer, which is the most complex component to modify due to its intricate process of synthesis. In this research, we develop a protocol to assist with hierarchy and data update tasks, including a method to determine whether to correct errors in the DNA information layer or update the hierarchy, as well as a protocol for exchanging information with the DNA information layer. By implementing these changes, we have successfully reduced the duration of data update processes and eliminated the need to synthesize an unnecessary amount of DNA. Moreover, our scheme has the capability to assist with hierarchy and data update tasks and has been found to provide optimal performance when used with a conventional memory hierarchy.

An innovative approach has been taken to create a high-speed solver for the shallow water equations, a fundamental set of conservation laws, by limiting the analysis to a specific subset of the solution space while employing artificial neural networks to estimate missing information. 
The simplified framework, which includes only the x-components of the momentum and depth-averaged velocity equations, allows for a significant decrease in the computational time to solve the full system of equations by at least an order of magnitude while maintaining the same level of accuracy in the results. 
The performance of this method has been evaluated and compared to the traditional finite volume solver used as a reference, yielding approximately 10 times the speed of the reference solver for a wide range of test cases, including both linear and nonlinear scenarios.

High-dynamic-range photography, which combines multiple photos taken at varying exposure levels to produce a single image with a wider dynamic range, has become a popular camera feature. However, the effectiveness of HDR photography relies heavily on several factors, including how exposure is set and images are combined. In order to improve HDR photography results, researchers have been analyzing and optimizing various aspects of it, although there's limited information available about how to set optimal exposure levels and image fusion methods. In order to address this gap, researchers have an idea to automate HDR photography by setting ideal exposure levels and a method to combine images, which they call HDR Refining. In order to evaluate HDR Refining, they created an algorithm to set exposure levels and image fusion methods based on principles of HDR photography, which they call HDR Evaluation. When they applied HDR Evaluation to multiple HDR photography scenarios, they found that their method could set better exposure levels than standard methods, which in turn led to better HDR photography results. In order to further improve HDR photography results, they also found that modifying HDR photography algorithms to set exposure levels and combine images based on image content could produce even better results. In order to test this idea, they created an enhanced HDR photography algorithm called Enhanced HDR, which they used to test on multiple scenarios and found that it could produce better results than standard HDR photography algorithms. In order to further analyze Enhanced HDR, they also created an algorithm to evaluate it called Enhanced HDR Evaluation, which they used to test on multiple scenarios and found

In recent years, there has been a significant shift in focusing on causal learning within neural networks, and it now occupies a central role in machine learning. Causal models, which incorporate graphs to represent relationships between variables, have become a fundamental aspect of learning and navigation within neural networks. Despite the wealth of research in this area, the field remains fragmented, with isolated contributions from various fields such as graph neural networks, reinforcement learning, and optimization. Our work aims to bridge this gap by exploring the connection between neural networks and causal models through the lens of learning and navigation, as we investigate cutting-edge research and emerging trends in the field. In the process, we re-imagine some of the existing research through the lens of learning and navigation, and conclude by discussing the promising directions and open issues in the field.

Given a oriented manifold $M^n$, it is possible to define a complex structure on it, provided that certain cohomological constraints are met. These conditions can be seen as a version of the b-principle applied to the statement of the Nash-Kuiper theorem, which in turn is a variant of the Arf-invariant sectionability criterion. This process also yields an alternative proof of the Mumford conjecture. 

However, being able to define a complex structure on $M^n$ is not equivalent to being able to submerge a complex structure into $M^n$, a fact that is demonstrated by an example based on the non-submersible complex structure discovered by Glorius. 

Moreover, some recent findings by Pardon, Pflow, Sustich, and Tessler show that certain types of complex structures in $4k$ dimensional spaces cannot be submerged into $2k$ dimensional manifolds, which in turn cannot have a complex structure of the same type, a result that can be seen as a more sophisticated version of the b-principle. 

All of these results can be found in chapter 5 of Pardon, Pflow, Sustich, and Tessler's research paper. 

It's worth noting that the research of Pardon, Pflow, Sustich, and Tessler relies on the b-principle, which was initially proposed by the Panoramic Team, and the paper in question provides a detailed analysis of the b-principle

The simulation of cardiac mechanics involves the resolution of complex fluid dynamics and electromechanical interactions, which can be computationally costly to model accurately, especially when considering large-scale simulations, such as those at the organ level, and with emerging real-time applications. Due to the demanding nature of these simulations, there is a growing need for efficient and scalable numerical methods to solve the underlying partial differential equations (PDEs). In our study, we compared and analyzed several multilevel preconditioning strategies for solving the cardiac mechanics problem, specifically using the Navier-Stokes equations and the monodomain model. We evaluated and validated different numerical parameters for three multilevel preconditioning techniques, including the use of specific solvers and smoothing parameters, which helped us develop a framework for benchmarking and validation. Utilizing our developed framework, we conducted a comprehensive comparison of 12 multilevel preconditioning configurations across two simulation scenarios, assessing their performance based on solution residuals, computational time, and accuracy. Our results showed that the most efficient and accurate solutions were obtained using a combination of the Craig-Copperthalev and GMRES solvers with a high degree of smoothing, resulting in significant improvements in the solution of the fluid mechanics component, which can lead to a 8-fold reduction in simulation time. Moreover, our findings highlighted the importance of carefully selecting numerical parameters to achieve optimal performance, as well as the potential benefits of multilevel preconditioning for the electromechanical model, particularly in simulations featuring fibrillation

We investigate a model of a random agent dispersal where an individual can move into a grid of size $N\times N$ if at high enough probability it manages to navigate through the obstacles, represented by a random field of size $N\times N$. The speed of an individual in a particular grid cell is determined by a Bernoulli trial with success probability $\epsilon$, with independent draws for each cell. The aim is to derive the probability density function of the random variable that represents the squared displacement of an individual after $K$ steps, dispersed among all possible scenarios of the random field of obstacles. The key findings include: as the number of steps $K$ tends to infinity, the probability density function of the random variable that represents the squared displacement of an individual approaches a density function that is proportional to $(x/N^2)^\frac{2}{\gamma}$ for a specific range of values, with the power-law index $\gamma$ equal to 1.76; the average squared displacement of an individual after $K$ steps is proportional to $N^2$; the distribution of the density of obstacles affects the power-law index $\gamma$, the mean density of obstacles affects the mean squared displacement, with the effect on the latter being more pronounced; with a given distribution of the density of obstacles, as $N$ increases, the probability density function of the random variable that represents the squared displacement of an individual changes from a delta function to a power-law density function;

We have developed a general mathematical framework to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of optical resonators, describing the phenomenon through a comprehensive set of equations that incorporate both the linear coupling coefficients and the mode-specific phase-matching conditions, in addition to the effects of losses and Kerr nonlinearity. We have demonstrated the applicability of our model by applying it to a representative photonic crystal nanobeam cavity and compared our results to numerical simulations, showing excellent agreement and highlighting the significance of proper mesh resolution in numerical simulations. Furthermore, we have examined the conditions under which our model yields reliable results, including the effects of geometrical variations and the number of optical modes considered. We believe our theoretical framework to be a valuable tool for designing and analyzing the nonlinear interactions of optical modes within photonic structures.

In 2002, Tobiska and Tsai discovered that a turbulent fluid flow at a low Reynolds number contained random patterns, which they termed "chaotic self-similarity". They proposed a model featuring a fractal boundary layer to accurately represent and calculate local and global flow characteristics. A recent study used Tobiska and Tsai's model to generate synthetic data representing turbulent fluid flows at various Reynolds numbers, and it was found to effectively match real flow data when compared using PSD and RE methods. Another study used Tobiska and Tsai's model to create an training dataset for a deep learning algorithm, which was then utilized to generate high-resolution flow images from lower-resolution ones, and was found to be highly effective in enhancing the resolution of real flow images.

For large language models to truly be considered sophisticated, they must be able
to excel in endless tasks they've never encountered before. To create a setting
where models can thrive in unlimited contexts, we've developed the L2Explorer
ecosystem, a cutting-edge, limitless reinforcement learning evaluation framework
featuring a dynamic web interface and a well-organized codebase for developers
to craft and submit challenging problems for models to resolve. With L2Explorer,
we've established a list of rigorous benchmarks to assess a model's ability to
adapt in an unlimited scenario and invest heavily in promoting the ecosystem
through grants and by assembling a community of contributors, including problem
creators, model developers, and donors to support the project financially.

In declarative processes, monitoring and exploration are both crucial tasks to ensure progress towards goals and to investigate possible paths. Our approach, designed for process languages with variables, builds on top of an established method [9] by incorporating a new way of comparing sequences, and with that, a new way of defining process relations. This, in turn, enables the monitoring of process properties defined using certain process relations. Additionally, we provide an algorithm for a specific exploration strategy, known as depth-first, and a more general way to compare sequences that allows for the monitoring of process properties defined using process relations that are not necessarily process equivalences. All the process relations and sequence comparisons we consider can be implemented using only the process and relation operators, without the need for additional comparison functions. This results in processes and relations being compared using the process relations themselves, and this in turn results in processes and relations being treated as black boxes. This treatment promotes process and relation abstraction, allowing processes and relations to be described in a way that does not reveal their internal workings, as long as the process relations used to do so are public knowledge. This is particularly useful in situations where processes and relations contain business secrets or are too complex to be easily defined.

We analyze the geometric structure of a parameter space, which is defined by a system of polynomial equations and inequalities. We examine both the scenario where the parameters are part of the coefficients and the scenario where the parameters are part of the variables. We investigate the algebraic approach of defining this space as the zero set of given functions, taking into account the absolute value of certain functions. We then explore an equivalent analytic approach using the Gaussian norm, taking care to handle the case where the space has boundary. We demonstrate that in the context of polynomial systems, both the algebraic and analytic approaches are equivalent, by constructing an isomorphism between the COX rings and the analytic ring, and we find that they are isomorphic as algebras. We apply this result to study the geometric properties of the parameter space, including its dimension, regularity, and Krull dimension, and we show that these properties are invariant under the change from the algebraic to the analytic formulation. We also investigate the effects of adding transcendental parameters to the space, and we find that this is equivalent to extending the ring to which the space is compactified. We further examine a specific example, which is a system of polynomial equations with parameters, and we discuss its applications to geometry and algebraic geometry.

The relationship between the stellar mass ($M_*$) and star formation rate ($SFR$) of galaxies is well established and indicates that more massive galaxies have lower specific star formation rates. The mechanism responsible for the reversal of the positive correlation between the growth of bulges and the decline of star formation, particularly above $M_* \approx 10^{10.2} M_\sun$, has puzzled astronomers for a long time. Using a large data set that includes multiple components of galaxies and their star formation rates, we investigated the course of this transformation through the assembly history of galaxies and their bulge and disk components. The results reveal that the reversal of the M*-SFR relation and the cessation of bulge growth and star formation occurred at $t \approx 2.5$ Gyr, when the universe was $30\%$ older, and coincided with the peak of major mergers. During this period, the formation of bulges and the decline of star formation reached their maximum rates, indicating a connection between the influence of major mergers, the formation of bulges, and the shutdown of star formation. The reversal of the M*-SFR relation also coincided with the peak of morphological transformation, marked by an increase in bulge-to-total mass ratio, and the growth of bulge stopped once the peak was reached. This study focuses on investigating sentiment in another language, where the same is not known about the task to be performed on Swedish text. Two aspects are investigated: the influence of performing a sentiment analysis on Swedish text and the impact of conducting the analysis on English text, using a combination of methods such as monolingual and bilingual models, to determine if there's a correlation between the two tasks. The research reveals that there is a connection between the two tasks, with the condition that the same be done with Swedish text. Additionally, it was discovered that the same was more accurate when the task was performed on English text, with the inclusion of multilingual models showing a significant improvement. A simple model was also found to excel in the same way in both Finnish and Italian, with the inclusion of multilingual models leading to a significant improvement. Notably, the same was more difficult to train for many languages such as French and German.

X-ray images contain valuable clinical information that can be utilized for predictive modeling, even without human interpretation. In the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, an analysis was conducted of 117 chest X-ray images belonging to 25 ICU patients, with a focus on quantifying and qualifying the image features that indicated a high risk of severe disease progression. A machine learning-based method was applied to extract and rank the most critical image characteristics associated with prolonged ICU stay. Notably, the analysis revealed that the location and pattern of lung opacities correlated with prolonged ICU stay, with the middle lung zones being the most critical area of interest. Furthermore, the study found that the presence of featureless lung opacities and the absence of tree-like pattern opacities were also key indicators of severe disease progression. By interpreting the results within the context of existing research on lung pathology and X-ray image analysis, this study provides a foundation for further exploration of predictive modeling that can forecast the risk of severe disease progression directly from X-ray images.

Given a covering map p: K -> X and a simplicial complex K, we can define a simplicial structure on the quotient space X. In the process, X is represented as a set of simplices, each linked to their corresponding simplices in K through the covering map p. We can then identify the simplicial complexes that can be realized in this manner and investigate how the properties of the covering map p affect the topology of X. We also examine how this relationship changes when the covering map p is updated to a global covering map p: K -> X. We find that the presence of a global covering map p: K -> X is sufficient to ensure that X has a certain number of locally defined open sets, each corresponding to a specific simplex in K. We then use this information to demonstrate that X can be given a simplicial structure equivalent to the one defined by the global covering map p: K -> X. We also consider how this relationship changes when the covering map p: K -> X is updated to a covering map p: K -> X. Recently generated adversarial examples have been found to significantly impair the performance of visual association detection on real-world data, indicating the existence of a substantial number of easily misclassified positive samples in current datasets. To address this issue, the authors propose a method to progressively refine the classification of these susceptible positives by applying a hard negative mining technique and incorporating a probability correction to enhance the confidence in correct classifications. In the proposed framework, a subset of the most challenging sample pairs is selectively identified and removed from further consideration as potential associations. A probability estimation module then assigns a confidence value to each remaining pair, with those exceeding a set confidence threshold deemed authentic associations. The authors demonstrate that this method can effectively raise the confidence of correct classifications to a level of at least 0.9, with the number of confidently identified associations being maximally increased by 13.4% on the VGG16 model and 16.7% on the ResNet50 model for the VCR dataset and 4.8% on the VGG16 model and 11.3% on the ResNet50 model for the Visual Genome dataset.

We're investigating the construction of galaxy bulges by observing a galaxy cluster that existed about 12 billion years ago, during a period when the universe was forming. By studying the galaxies in this cluster, we're uncovering how galaxies built their central bulge regions and how they were shaped by gravitational interactions and the accumulation of gas. Certain galaxies in this cluster are notable for containing both actively forming star regions and centrally concentrated bulge areas, and by studying these galaxies, we're able to track the movement of gas and the formation of stars over time. We're using a supercomputer to simulate the development of these galaxies and test their evolution, and our findings suggest that the formation of bulge areas in galaxies can occur through the collision of galaxies, even in calm environments, and that these collisions can influence the distribution of stars and the formation of stars over time.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia and Mexico have been incorporated into existing networks of neutron monitors, providing a more comprehensive view of the Earth's surroundings with respect to solar neutron detectors. To analyze the positioning of these new detectors, a simulation of the November 7, 2004, solar proton event was conducted by re-computing the decomposition of solar protons. The re-computation showed that the event could have been detected by a detector positioned at the Earth's surface in Antarctica, and further investigation was made possible by the presence of deep ice at the AMANDA site. Barriers such as the Antarctic ice sheet pose a significant challenge for neutron decomposition detectors, yet our simulation indicates that the density of the ice has a minimal impact on the detection of wide-beam protons. 

Our simulation of the November 7, 2004, event also included re-estimating the energy spectrum of protons, which revealed that the decomposition of neutrons caused by cosmic rays could have been produced at higher altitudes than previously thought, specifically within the range of 5500 to 6000 meters. Notably, this finding aligns with the elevation of the AMANDA site, situated at an altitude of approximately 2830 meters above sea level in the Antarctic Ice Sheet.
